query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled, moderate-temperature annealing step below the glass transition temperature (Tg) in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys induces partial structural relaxation that increases medium-range order and decreases free volume, thereby improving both the glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state by delaying the onset of crystallization.
generation.material_initial_state: A rapidly quenched, as-cast amorphous phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy with excess free volume and a metastable atomic configuration.
generation.intervention: Apply a thermal/thermomechanical annealing treatment at a temperature 50–100 K below the measured Tg for a short, controlled duration (e.g., approximately 10 minutes) immediately after quenching.
generation.conditions: This treatment is expected to be effective when applied to as-quenched samples, provided the annealing temperature is carefully controlled within the moderate sub-Tg window; it may not yield the desired improvements if the temperature is set too low (insufficient for structural relaxation) or too high (approaching Tg, risking premature crystallization).
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced medium-range ordering and reduced free volume resulting from partial atomic rearrangements during the annealing process.
generation.mechanism: The annealing step promotes defect and free volume annihilation, leading to a relaxed amorphous structure that is less prone to nucleation and growth of crystals during subsequent heating, thereby increasing the crystallization onset temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to as-cast samples, annealed samples will exhibit a higher crystallization onset temperature (as measured by DSC) and improved resistance to crystallization upon heating, indicating enhanced thermal stability and glass-forming ability.
generation.baseline: The as-cast amorphous state produced by rapid quenching without any subsequent thermal relaxation treatment.
generation.boundary: The intervention may not be effective if the annealing temperature is not within the 50–100 K sub-Tg range, if the hold time is too short to permit significant relaxation, or if compositional variations lead to markedly different diffusion kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in crystallization onset temperature and the optimal duration of annealing require further calibration; quantitative effects may vary with alloy composition and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy samples using an identical rapid-quenching process. Subject one set to the proposed moderate-temperature annealing step (50–100 K below Tg for ~10 minutes) while the other set remains untreated. Use differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to measure the crystallization onset temperature and glass transition characteristics of both sets, and perform X-ray diffraction to verify the amorphous nature pre- and post-treatment.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in crystallization onset temperature or demonstrate improved resistance to crystallization compared to the untreated control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

This principle underscores the preferential formation of the amorphous state in materials with high configurational entropy, which correlates with a greater glass-forming ability. Therefore, configuration entropy is pivotal in predicting the glass-forming ability of AMAs and ensuring their stability as noncrystalline solids.

The observation of amorphous particles transforming into a crystalline phase validates that the amorphous phase is metastable and forms under kinetic control, whereas the crystalline structure is the thermodynamically favored one [], and thermodynamic control is dominant when activation energy barriers are overcome by heating.

In conclusion, we discovered an unusual glass-to-glass transition in a NbNiZrTiCo HEMG with a large exotherm. It was found that the high-entropy effect could dynamically elevate the MG to a high-energy glass state and thermodynamically enable the glass-to-glass transition from the high-energy glass state to a low-energy glass state during heating. Through this simple and non-destructive heat-treating process, this glass-to-glass transition can alter the modulus and hardness more remarkably than rejuvenation by thermal cycling or mechanical deformation. Besides, the HEMGs might also be applied as promising energetic materials, where the large anomalous exotherm may contribute to their combustion heats and lower the ignition temperatures. In addition, the obtained low-energy state HEMGs exhibit excellent thermal stability. The present results provide an opportunity for further tuning the glass structure and property and addressing the fundamental issues of MGs.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC9023469) showed how high-entropy effects in metallic glasses can produce glass-to-glass transitions that improve glass-forming ability (GFA) and elevate thermal stability. Efforts then shifted toward data-driven design (PMC11480990), where machine learning–based models were developed to tackle complex high-entropy and amorphous alloy compositions and predict GFA. More recently, investigations of phosphorus-rich high-entropy alloys under varying cooling rates (PMC11642357) confirmed that rapid quenching drives a deep undercooling and increases the fraction of amorphous structure, but a systematic route to stabilize the glassy phase and retard crystallization has not yet been conclusively established.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear which single, reliable material intervention (beyond merely changing composition) can simultaneously boost glass-forming ability and impede crystallization during subsequent thermal exposure in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys, especially across a range of practical processing routes and service temperatures.
decision.lever: Apply a moderate-temperature annealing step (e.g., 50–100 K below the measured glass transition temperature) to partially relax the as-quenched amorphous structure, thereby stabilizing medium-range ordering and reducing excess free volume.
decision.why: Prior data (particularly from rapid-quench studies of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys) highlight that the as-cast amorphous state can crystallize prematurely upon heating. A short, controlled annealing can quell the primary devitrification pathway by promoting defect annihilation and local atomic rearrangement. This targeted relaxation can improve the onset temperature for crystallization—observed in glass-to-glass transitions in other high-entropy metallic glasses (PMC9023469)—while machine-learning predictions (PMC11480990) and controlled cooling experiments (PMC11642357) underscore the importance of managing structural relaxation for enhanced GFA and thermal stability.
